questions.title: Vitamin B12 absorption requirement
questions.question: Absorption of vitamin B12 requires the presence of:

explanations.A: Correct. Intrinsic factor, secreted by the gastric parietal cells, binds vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in the gut lumen and carries it to the terminal ileum, where the intrinsic-factor-B12 complex is recognised by a specific receptor and taken up by endocytosis. Without intrinsic factor, dietary B12 cannot be absorbed in adequate amounts regardless of how much is ingested, which is why autoimmune destruction of parietal cells (as in pernicious anaemia) causes B12 deficiency even on a normal diet. This absorption pathway is unique to B12 among the vitamins and is the reason B12 deficiency, unlike most other vitamin deficiencies, can arise from a gastric rather than a dietary problem.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pepsin is a gastric protease that digests dietary protein; it plays no specific role in carrying B12 to its ileal absorption site.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thiamin is vitamin B1, an unrelated water-soluble vitamin with its own separate absorption pathway; it is not required for B12 absorption.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since neither pepsin nor thiamin is the factor B12 absorption depends on, combining them is also wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that intrinsic factor is required for vitamin B12 absorption.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Intrinsic factor", p23

questions.title: Chemical nature of intrinsic factor
questions.question: Intrinsic factor is chemically a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A peptide is a short chain of amino acids; intrinsic factor is a much larger molecule than a simple peptide.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A mucopolysaccharide is a carbohydrate polymer (a glycosaminoglycan); intrinsic factor is not built on this backbone.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intrinsic factor does have a protein backbone, but plain "protein" omits the carbohydrate side chains attached to it, which is the more complete and correct classification.
explanations.D: Correct. Intrinsic factor is a glycoprotein, secreted by the gastric parietal cells alongside hydrochloric acid. Its carbohydrate side chains, attached to a protein backbone, are part of what gives it the specific three-dimensional shape needed to bind vitamin B12 with high affinity in the gut lumen. This glycoprotein-B12 complex then survives transit through the small intestine until it reaches its dedicated receptor in the terminal ileum.

questions.learning_objective: Identify intrinsic factor as a glycoprotein secreted by gastric parietal cells.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Glycoprotein", p23

questions.title: Causes of vitamin B12 deficiency
questions.question: Deficiency of vitamin B12 can occur because of:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Intestinal malabsorption (for example after ileal resection, since the terminal ileum is the specific absorption site) is a genuine cause of B12 deficiency, but it is not the only one listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own. Atrophy of the gastric mucosa removes the parietal cells that secrete intrinsic factor, and so is also a genuine cause, but again not the only one.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. Simple dietary lack of B12, as in a strict vegan diet with no supplementation, is a genuine cause too, but the question asks for all of the listed causes together.
explanations.D: Correct. Vitamin B12 deficiency can arise from any point of failure along its path from diet to tissue: too little intake, loss of the gastric intrinsic-factor-secreting mucosa, or failure of intestinal absorption even when intrinsic factor is present and intake is adequate. All three listed mechanisms (intestinal malabsorption, gastric mucosal atrophy, and decreased intake) are recognised, independent causes of B12 deficiency, which is why the complete answer is all of them together rather than any single one.

questions.learning_objective: List the three recognised mechanisms of vitamin B12 deficiency: decreased intake, gastric mucosal atrophy, and intestinal malabsorption.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: All of these", p24

questions.title: Functions requiring ascorbic acid
questions.question: Ascorbic acid is required to synthesise all of the following except:

explanations.A: Correct. Bile pigments (bilirubin and its derivatives) come from haem catabolism, a pathway that does not require vitamin C. Ascorbic acid does participate in the synthesis of bile acids (via hepatic cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase), of catecholamines such as epinephrine (as a cofactor for dopamine beta-hydroxylase) and of collagen (as the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase), so bile pigments are the one listed synthesis that is not vitamin-C dependent. This is why vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) produces connective-tissue and catecholamine-related problems but does not itself disturb bile pigment metabolism or cause jaundice.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bile acid synthesis does require ascorbic acid as a cofactor, so this is one of the syntheses vitamin C supports, not the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Epinephrine synthesis does require ascorbic acid as a cofactor for dopamine beta-hydroxylase, so this is also not the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Collagen synthesis is vitamin C's best-known dependent process, via prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation, so this is not the exception either.

questions.learning_objective: Identify bile pigment synthesis as independent of vitamin C, in contrast to bile acid, catecholamine and collagen synthesis.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Bile pigments", p24

questions.title: Vitamin C and intestinal iron absorption
questions.question: Vitamin C enhances the intestinal absorption of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitamin C does enhance one of the listed minerals' absorption.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vitamin C has no established role in intestinal iodine absorption.
explanations.C: Correct. Vitamin C reduces dietary ferric iron (Fe3+) to the more soluble and more readily absorbed ferrous form (Fe2+) in the gut lumen, and also forms a soluble chelate with iron that resists precipitation, both of which enhance intestinal iron absorption. This is why vitamin C-rich foods or supplements taken alongside iron-rich meals are recommended to improve iron uptake, particularly for non-haem (plant-source) iron. This effect is specific to iron among the common dietary minerals and is one of vitamin C's clinically applied functions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin C has no established role in intestinal potassium absorption.

questions.learning_objective: State that vitamin C enhances intestinal iron absorption by reducing ferric to ferrous iron.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Iron", p24

questions.title: Which cobalamin form contains cyanide
questions.question: The following has cyanide:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Adenosylcobalamin (adenylcobamide) is one of the two active coenzyme forms of B12 used in the body and does not carry a cyanide group.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is not a standard cobalamin form recognised as the cyanide-containing one; the correct name for the cyanide-bound form is cyanocobalamin, i.e. vitamin B12 itself as commonly supplied.
explanations.C: Correct. "Vitamin B12" as commercially and pharmaceutically supplied is cyanocobalamin, the stable, cyanide-bound form of cobalamin used in supplements and injections because it is chemically stable for storage. The cyanide group is not part of the naturally active coenzyme forms (methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin) but is added during purification to stabilise the vitamin for pharmaceutical use, and the body then converts cyanocobalamin to the active coenzyme forms. This is why "vitamin B12" is the option correctly identified as cyanide-containing among the listed cobalamin forms.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Methylcobalamin is the other active coenzyme form of B12 (used by methionine synthase) and does not carry a cyanide group.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cyanocobalamin as the cyanide-containing, pharmaceutically supplied form of vitamin B12.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Vitamin B12", p25

questions.author_notes: Original stem's option (a) OCR'd as "Adenylcobamide" -- read as adenosylcobalamin, one of B12's two active coenzyme forms.

questions.title: Pyridoxine deficiency and convulsions
questions.question: Pyridoxine deficiency may lead to convulsions as it is needed for the synthesis of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Essential fatty acids (EFA) are not synthesised in the body at all (they must come from the diet) and are unrelated to pyridoxine's convulsion-preventing role.
explanations.B: Correct. Pyridoxal phosphate, the active coenzyme form of pyridoxine (vitamin B6), is required by glutamate decarboxylase to convert the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate into the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA. When B6 is deficient, this conversion falls, glutamate accumulates relative to GABA, and the resulting shift toward excitation over inhibition in the central nervous system produces convulsions, a finding described especially in infants. This mechanistic link between pyridoxine and GABA synthesis is why pyridoxine-responsive seizures are treated by administering the vitamin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) is a component of folate's structure, not a product whose synthesis explains pyridoxine-deficiency convulsions.
explanations.D: Incorrect. S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is the body's universal methyl donor, synthesised from methionine and ATP; its synthesis is not the mechanism linking pyridoxine deficiency to convulsions.

questions.learning_objective: Explain pyridoxine-deficiency convulsions through impaired GABA synthesis from glutamate.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: GABA", p25

questions.title: Dietary source rich in vitamin C
questions.question: This is a rich source for vitamin C:

explanations.A: Correct. Lemon, like other citrus fruits, is a well-known dietary source rich in vitamin C (ascorbic acid), which is why citrus fruits are classically recommended to prevent or treat scurvy. Fresh fruits and vegetables in general are the main dietary sources of vitamin C, since, unlike most other mammals, humans cannot synthesise it and must obtain it entirely from the diet. Rice, egg and milk, by contrast, contain negligible amounts of vitamin C, since it is not present in appreciable quantities in cereal grains or in most animal-derived foods.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rice is a cereal grain and contains essentially no vitamin C.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Egg is an animal-derived food and is a poor source of vitamin C.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Milk is an animal-derived food and is a poor source of vitamin C.

questions.learning_objective: Identify citrus fruits such as lemon as a rich dietary source of vitamin C.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Lemon", p26

questions.title: Hypertonic solution for red blood cells
questions.question: Which of the following solutions is hypertonic for red blood cells?

explanations.A: Correct. Normal saline, 0.9% NaCl, is isotonic to red blood cells and is the reference point against which every other concentration is judged. Since 1.0% NaCl carries a higher non-penetrating solute concentration than this 0.9% isotonic reference, it is hypertonic to the red blood cell: water leaves the cell by osmosis down its own concentration gradient, and the cell shrinks (crenates). Both 0.10% and 0.5% NaCl, by contrast, are more dilute than the 0.9% reference and so are hypotonic, not hypertonic, drawing water into the cell instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 0.9% NaCl is the isotonic reference itself, producing no net water movement or volume change, not the hypertonic solution being asked for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.10% NaCl is far more dilute than the isotonic 0.9% reference, making it markedly hypotonic, not hypertonic; it would swell, not shrink, the cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 0.5% NaCl is still more dilute than the isotonic 0.9% reference, making it hypotonic, not hypertonic.

questions.learning_objective: Rank saline concentrations against the 0.9% isotonic reference to identify a hypertonic solution for red blood cells.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: 1.0% NaCl", p35

questions.title: Which is not an oxygen-derived free radical
questions.question: Which of the following is not an oxygen derived free radical (ROS)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Superoxide anion (O2 with an unpaired electron) is one of the primary oxygen-derived free radicals (ROS), generated for example as a byproduct of the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hydroxyl radical is an oxygen-derived free radical, and the most reactive one of the group, typically generated from hydrogen peroxide via the Fenton reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hydrogen peroxide is grouped with the oxygen-derived free radicals (ROS) because, although not itself a radical in the strict sense, it readily generates the hydroxyl radical.
explanations.D: Correct. Nitric oxide is a genuine free radical, since it carries an unpaired electron, but it is nitrogen-centred rather than oxygen-derived, and is classed separately as a reactive nitrogen species (RNS) rather than one of the oxygen-derived ROS (superoxide, hydroxyl radical, hydrogen peroxide). This distinction between the oxygen-derived ROS family and the separately classed nitrogen-centred radicals such as nitric oxide is exactly what this question is testing. Nitric oxide has its own distinct physiological roles, including vasodilation and neurotransmission, that are unrelated to the oxidative-injury role of the ROS family.

questions.topic: Oxygen Toxicity and Free Radical Injury
questions.subtopic: Free radical definition, sources and effects
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the oxygen-derived free radicals (ROS) from nitric oxide, a separately classed nitrogen-centred radical.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Nitric oxide", p87

questions.title: Substrate class that cannot form free radicals
questions.question: Which of the following can't form free radicals?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Xenobiotics (foreign chemicals, including many drugs and toxins) can generate free radicals during their metabolism, for example through cytochrome P450-mediated reactions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Molecular oxygen is the direct source of the oxygen-derived free radicals (superoxide, hydroxyl radical, hydrogen peroxide).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lipids can propagate free-radical chain reactions through lipid peroxidation, particularly the polyunsaturated fatty acids.
explanations.D: Correct. Carbohydrates, unlike oxygen, lipids and xenobiotics, are not a recognised source of free radical formation in this bank's teaching. Their oxidation and metabolism proceed through pathways (such as glycolysis and the citric acid cycle) that do not themselves generate radical intermediates in the way lipid peroxidation or xenobiotic metabolism do. This makes carbohydrates the correct exception among the four listed biomolecule classes.

questions.topic: Oxygen Toxicity and Free Radical Injury
questions.subtopic: Free radical definition, sources and effects
questions.learning_objective: Identify carbohydrates as the biomolecule class that does not itself form free radicals, unlike oxygen, lipids and xenobiotics.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Carbohydrates", p87

questions.title: Which is not an effect of free radicals
questions.question: Which of the following is not an effect of free radicals?

options.C: Loss of biological activity of some enzymes

explanations.A: Incorrect. Free radicals damage cell membranes through lipid peroxidation of membrane phospholipids, which is one of their recognised effects.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Free radicals damage DNA and cause mutations, predisposing to cancer, which is also a recognised effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Free radicals oxidise functional groups on enzymes and other proteins, causing loss of their biological activity, which is likewise a recognised effect.
explanations.D: Correct. Protein glycosylation is the non-enzymatic attachment of a sugar molecule to a protein, as seen in glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c); it proceeds by a separate, non-oxidative chemical mechanism and is not itself caused by free radicals. This makes it the correct exception among the four listed options, each of which describes damage attributed to free-radical activity except this one. Recognising that glycosylation and oxidative (free-radical) damage are mechanistically distinct processes is the specific distinction this question is testing.

questions.topic: Oxygen Toxicity and Free Radical Injury
questions.subtopic: Free radical definition, sources and effects
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish free-radical (oxidative) damage from non-oxidative protein glycosylation.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Protein glycosylation", p88

questions.title: Lipid most vulnerable to free-radical damage
questions.question: Which of the following lipid is most affected by free radicals?

explanations.A: Correct. Polyunsaturated fatty acids carry multiple carbon-carbon double bonds, and the carbon atoms between those double bonds (the allylic positions) hold hydrogen atoms that are especially easy for a free radical to abstract, initiating a self-propagating chain reaction called lipid peroxidation. This makes polyunsaturated fatty acids the lipid class most vulnerable to free-radical damage, since more double bonds mean more of these easily abstracted hydrogens along the chain. This vulnerability is why polyunsaturated membrane phospholipids are a principal target of oxidative injury in cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-carbon double bonds and lack the easily abstracted allylic hydrogens, making them far more resistant to free-radical (peroxidative) damage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Monounsaturated fatty acids have only one double bond, giving them intermediate but still much lower vulnerability than the multiple double bonds of polyunsaturated fatty acids.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chain length alone (long chain fatty acids) is not what determines vulnerability to free-radical attack; the degree of unsaturation (number of double bonds) is the determining factor, and that is captured by option A, not this one.

questions.topic: Oxygen Toxicity and Free Radical Injury
questions.subtopic: Free radical definition, sources and effects
questions.learning_objective: Explain why polyunsaturated fatty acids are the lipid class most vulnerable to free-radical (peroxidative) damage.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Polyunsaturated fatty acids", p88
